fig1_ke_vs_speed.svg: $KE=\tfrac12mV^2$ (kinetic_energy) for three vehicle-scale masses. The curvature carries the practical content: a 1500 kg car at 20 m/s holds 300 kJ, but at 40 m/s it holds 1200 kJ — four times as much for twice the speed. Braking from 40 to 20 m/s alone sheds 900 kJ, all of which the brakes must turn into heat. This term is usually negligible next to internal energy, which is why closed-system problems drop it, but it dominates in nozzles and in collisions.
fig2_speed_after_work.svg: The work-energy theorem run backwards: given the net work delivered to a 1500 kg body, what speed results (speed_after_work, from $\tfrac12mV_2^2=\tfrac12mV_1^2+W$)? Because the answer is a square root, the returns diminish sharply — the first 300 kJ takes a body from rest to 20.0 m/s, while the second 300 kJ adds only 8.3 m/s more. The same work does less for a body that is already fast.
